Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this article we study the local controllability of the one-dimensional Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes equation, that is Cahn-Hilliard-Burgers’ equation, around a certain steady state using a localized interior control acting only in the concentration equation. To do it, we first linearize the nonlinear equation around the steady state. The linearized system turns out to be a system coupled between second order and fourth order parabolic equations and the control acts in the fourth order parabolic equation. The null controllability of the linearized system is obtained by a duality argument proving an observability inequality. To prove the observability inequality, a new Carleman inequality for the coupled system is derived. Next, using the source term method, it is shown that the null controllability of the linearized system with non-homogeneous terms persists provided the non-homogeneous terms satisfy certain estimates in a suitable weighted space. Finally, using a Banach fixed point theorem in a suitable weighted space, the local controllability of the nonlinear system is obtained.

Key words and phrases: 
Controllability, Carleman estimates, source term method, fixed point argument
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
35M33, 35K61, 93B05, 93B07, 93C20

1. Introduction

The widely recognized Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes (CHNS) equation, introduced by Hohenberg and Halperin [[21], see also [18]], serves as a prominent model for describing the evolution of an incompressible isothermal mixture comprising two immiscible fluids. This model, also known as a diffuse interface model, replaces the sharp interface between the fluids with a diffuse interface by introducing an order parameter and takes dimensionless form in higher dimension as:

(1.1) {∂tϕ+𝐮⋅∇ϕ=div(m(ϕ)∇μ), in Ω×(0,T),μ=−Δ​ϕ+F′​(ϕ),∂t𝐮−div(ν(ϕ)D𝐮)+(𝐮⋅∇)𝐮+∇π=μ∇ϕ, in Ω×(0,T),div​𝐮=0, in ​Ω×(0,T),𝐮=0, on ​∂Ω×(0,T),∂ϕ∂𝐧=0,∂μ∂𝐧=0, on ​∂Ω×(0,T),𝐮⁡(0)=𝐮0,φ⁡(0)=φ0, in ​Ω,\left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}\phi+\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\mathrm{\phi}&=\text{div}(m(\mathrm{\phi})\nabla\mu),\,\,\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \mu&=-\Delta\mathrm{\phi}+F^{\prime}(\mathrm{\phi}),\\ \partial_{t}\mathbf{u}-\text{div}(\nu(\mathrm{\phi})\mathrm{D}\mathbf{u})+(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u}+\nabla\pi&=\mu\nabla\mathrm{\phi},\,\,\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \text{div}~\mathbf{u}&=0,\,\,\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \mathbf{u}&=0,\,\,\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \frac{\partial\mathrm{\phi}}{\partial\mathbf{n}}=0,\,\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial\mathbf{n}}&=0,\,\,\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \mathbf{u}(0)=\mathbf{u}_{0},\,\,\mathrm{\varphi}(0)&=\mathrm{\varphi}_{0},\,\,\text{ in }\Omega,\end{aligned}\right.

where 𝐮⁡(t,x)\mathbf{u}(t,\mathrm{x}) is the average velocity of the fluid and ϕ⁡(t,x)\mathrm{\phi}(t,\mathrm{x}) is the relative concentration of the fluid. Here, Ω\Omega is a bounded domain in ℝd,d≥2\mathbb{R}^{d},d\geq 2 with a sufficiently smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The density is taken as matched density, i.e., constant density, which is equal to 1. Moreover, mm is mobility of binary mixture, μ\mu is a chemical potential, π\pi is the pressure, ν\nu is the viscosity and FF is a double well potential. The symmetric part of the gradient of the flow velocity vector is denoted by D​𝐮\mathrm{D}\mathbf{u}, that is, D​𝐮\mathrm{D}\mathbf{u} is the strain tensor 12​(∇𝐮+(∇𝐮)⊤)\frac{1}{2}\left(\nabla\mathbf{u}+(\nabla\mathbf{u})^{\top}\right).
The existing theoretical literature, encompassing aspects such as well-posedness, strong solutions, optimal control problem, attractors and long-term behavior without being exhausted can be summarized in [15, 16, 2, 31, 28, 32, 27, 14, 1]. The controllability aspects of this coupled system has not been considered yet in the literature. Due to significance of this diffuse interface model in the fluid dynamics, we are interested to study its controllability properties.

To gain insights into the problem, we choose to explore a one dimensional version of the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes model, which is the Cahn-Hilliard-Burgers’ model. In particular, we consider the Cahn-Hilliard-Burgers’ model with constant mobility m⁡(ϕ)=1m(\phi)=1 and constant viscosity ν⁡(ϕ)=γ>0\nu(\phi)=\gamma>0 in QT=(0,T)×(0,1)Q_{T}=(0,T)\times(0,1), for any finite time T>0T>0, with a control hh acting in the concentration equation:

Our main results in the article are stated below. First, we have following null controllability result for the linearized system (1.9)–(1.11):

(w⁡(T,⋅),ψ⁡(T,⋅))=(0,0)in(L2​(0,1))2.\left(w(T,\cdot),\,\psi(T,\cdot)\right)=(0,0)\quad\mathrm{in}\quad(L^{2}(0,1))^{2}.

Further using a fixed point argument, we obtain the following result for the non-linear system:

Theorem 1.4.

Let (u¯,ϕ¯)(\overline{u},\overline{\phi}) be as mentioned in Remark 1.1 and let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be any open subset of (0,1)(0,1). For any T>0T>0, there exists a positive number μ\mu such that for any (w0,ψ0)∈(L2​(0,1))2,(w_{0},\psi_{0})\in(L^{2}(0,1))^{2}, with ‖(w0,ψ0)‖L2×L2≤μ,\left\|(w_{0},\psi_{0})\right\|_{L^{2}\times L^{2}}\leq\mu, there exists a control h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪))h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O})) such that the system (1.6) admits a solution (w,ψ)∈C⁡([0,T],L2​(0,1))∩L2​(0,T,H01​(0,1))×C⁡([0,T],L2​(0,1))∩L2​(0,T,H12)(w,\psi)\in C([0,T];L^{2}(0,1))\cap L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}_{0}(0,1))\times C([0,T];L^{2}(0,1))\cap L^{2}(0,T;H^{2}_{1}) satisfying

(w⁡(T,⋅),ψ⁡(T,⋅))=(0,0)in(L2​(0,1))2.\left(w(T,\cdot),\,\psi(T,\cdot)\right)=(0,0)\quad\mathrm{in}\quad(L^{2}(0,1))^{2}.

The proof of the interior null controllability of the linearized system (1.9)–(1.11) in Theorem 1.3 relies on proving an observability inequality for the solutions of the adjoint system. To prove the observability inequality, leveraging global Carleman estimates for the Cahn-Hilliard equation and Burgers’ equation, we first derive a unified Carleman estimate for our coupled system. This, in turn, facilitates the proof of null-controllability for the linearized system with an appropriate control cost of M​eM⁡(T+1Tm)Me^{M(T+\frac{1}{T^{m}})}. This step is pivotal for deducing local controllability results for the nonlinear model. Subsequently, we employ the source term method, specifically proving the null-controllability of the linear model (1.9)–(1.11) with suitably chosen source terms from a weighted Hilbert space where the weight function blows up as tt approaches T−T^{-}. Finally, employing the Banach fixed-point argument in a suitable weighted space, we establish local null-controllability for the nonlinear model and hence Theorem 1.4.

Let us mention some related works in this direction from the available literature. The controllability of parabolic equations using Carleman inequality has been studied in [13] in details. The fourth order parabolic equation, namely Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation, has been extensively appears in many works such as [9], [33], [6], [30]. In particular, in [6], the authors proved that the linear KS equation with Neumann boundary conditions is null-controllable by a control acting in some open subset of the domain. In [30], the author studied the boundary local null-controllability of the KS equation by utilizing the source term method (see [24]) followed by the Banach fixed point argument where a suitable control cost C​eC/TCe^{C/T} of the linearized model plays the crucial role. Similar strategy has been applied in [20] to study the boundary local null-controllability of a simplified stabilized KS system.

To include dispersive and extra dissipative effects in the KS equation, a coupled system containing fourth (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky-Korteweg-de Vries, in short KS-KdV equation) and second order parabolic (heat) equations, under the name of stabilized Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system has appeared for instance in [25]. The controllability of such system has been considered in several works, namely [10], [7], [8], [5], [22]. E. Cerpa, A. Mercado and A. F. Pazoto in [8] demonstrated the local null-controllability of Stabilized KS equation by means of localized interior control acting in the KS-KdV equation. Then, E. Cerpa and N. Carreño [5] proved the local null-controllability to the trajectories with a localized interior control exerted in the heat equation. Two different types of Carleman estimates for the linearized model followed by the inverse mapping theorem have been implemented to conclude their controllability results. We also point out that recently, the controllability of KS-KdV-transport model and KS-KdV-elliptic equation have been discussed in [23], [3] respectively.

The spirit of our work relies on that of [19, 8]. The fourth order parabolic equation of our system is similar to that of the equation considered in [19] with the same boundary conditions. However, unlike our case, [19] deals with only the fourth order parabolic equation and not a coupled system between fourth order and second order parabolic equations. Rather, in [8], a system coupled between a fourth order parabolic equation and a second order parabolic equation is considered. But the boundary condition for the fourth order equation is different than us. Thus, though the main strategy used to prove our result is classical and is similar to that of [19, 8], due to the presence of the coupling and the different boundary conditions, our results do not follow directly from any of the earlier works mentioned above. In fact, to handle the coupling between equations and the boundary conditions, we need to derive a new Carleman inequality to prove the observability inequality.

The novelty of our work is to deal with the coupling between second and fourth order parabolic equations with the boundary conditions and nonlinear terms and to obtain the controllability results. Even though the main strategy of the proof of our results is standard, each step of the proof has to be investigated due to the difficulty posed by the coupling and the boundary conditions and the nonlinear terms. For instance, a new Carleman inequality for the coupled system has to be derived for this system with a careful study on the weight functions applicable for both the second order and the forth order parabolic equations with the boundary conditions. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to study the controllability of the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier Stokes equation around a trajectory. Our results obtained here give an insight how to approach to study the controllability of the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier Stokes equation in more general set-up and in higher dimensions (see Section 7).

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we first study the well-posedness of the linear coupled system and its associated adjoint problem. Section 3 is devoted to prove a Carleman inequality associated to the solution of the adjoint problem. This is the main tool to prove the null controllability result for the linear coupled system in Section 4. First in Section 4.1, an observability inequality for the solution of the adjoint problem is established and consequently in Section 4.2, Theorem 1.3 is proved. Next, in Section 5, the null controllability of the linear coupled system with non-homogeneous terms from a suitable weighted space is proved. Finally, using a Banach fixed point argument, Theorem 1.4, the local null controllability of (1.6) is proved in Section 6. At the end, in Section 7, we mention a few open problems in this direction and possible extensions of our results.

Now we state the well-posedness result for the adjoint system (2.12). The proof of the theorem is similar to that of Theorem 2.2.

Theorem 2.4.

Moreover there exists a positive constant CC, depending on TT, such that

3. Carleman inequality

This section is devoted to the derivation of suitable Carleman estimate for the adjoint system (2.12) to deduce the required observability inequality. To do so, let us define the some useful weight functions.

Consider a non-empty open set 𝒪0⊂⊂𝒪\mathcal{O}_{0}\subset\subset\mathcal{O}. There exists a function ν∈C4​([0,1])\nu\in C^{4}([0,1]) such that

This theorem was proved in [19, Proposition 3.1], for the weight defined in (3.2) with m=1m=1. In order to prove Theorem 3.3, for the weight function defined in (3.2) with m>3m>3 one can follow the same steps as in the proof of [19, Proposition 3.1]. 4. Controllability of the linear system

This section is devoted to the proof of null controllability of the linearized model (1.9)–(1.10)–(1.11), that is Theorem 1.3. We know that the null controllability of (1.9)–(1.10)–(1.11) is equivalent to an observability inequality for the solutions of the adjoint system (2.12). In the sequel, we first prove the observability inequality using Carleman inequality obtained in Section 3. The observability inequality indeed gives the null controllability of the system (1.9)–(1.10)–(1.11) at any time T>0T>0 with a certain control cost. To obtain the specific control cost as mentioned in Theorem 1.3, next we split the proof of the controllability result in to two cases- one case is for 0<T<10<T<1 and the other case is for T≥1T\geq 1 and finally conclude the section with the proof of Theorem 1.3.

4.1. Observability inequality

To prove the observability inequality, we require the following lemma which can be obtained by using energy estimate.

5. Null controllability of the linearized model with nonhomogeneous source term

In this section, using the controllability and the control cost in (1.14) for the linear system without forcing term, we shall prove the null controllability of the linearized model with nonhomogeneous source provided the source lies in some suitable weighted spaces. The proof will be based on the so-called source term method developed in [24]. It is worth mentioning that in [24], the authors demonstrate the source term method with an associated control cost of the form C​eC/TCe^{C/T}. In contrast, the work [29] addresses a different type of control cost, more precisely C​eC/TlCe^{C/T^{l}} with l≥11l\geq 11 (see Lemma 4.1 and Section 4.3 in [29] for details), which we adopt in this work to obtain our result.

Recall that in Theorem 1.3, we have the null controllability of (1.9) in (L2​(0,1))2(L^{2}(0,1))^{2} at any time T>0T>0 with the control cost M​eM​T​eMTm{Me^{MT}e^{\frac{M}{T^{m}}}} given in (1.14) for some M>0M>0 independent of TT. In view of this, we introduce the following weighted spaces to handle the system with forcing terms.

6. Local null controllability of the nonlinear system

This section is devoted to the proof of our main results Theorem 1.4. In the previous section we have proved that linearized model (5.4) is null controllable whenever the source terms lie in the weighted space 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Using this result along with Banach fixed point theorem, we conclude the main result.

Let us recall the weighted spaces (5.3a), (5.3) and (5.3d).

Recall that due to Proposition 5.2 and Lemma 6.1, for any given (u,φ)∈𝒴(u,\varphi)\in\mathcal{Y}, there exists a control h(u,φ)∈𝒱h^{(u,\varphi)}\in\mathcal{V} such that (6.6) admits a unique solution (w(u,φ),ψ(u,φ))∈𝒴(w^{(u,\varphi)},\psi^{(u,\varphi)})\in\mathcal{Y} satisfying the null controllability condition (5.5) and the estimate (5.6) where f1=N1​(u,φ)f_{1}=N_{1}(u,\varphi) and f2=N2​(u,φ)f_{2}=N_{2}(u,\varphi).

In view of that, for R>0R>0, we set

𝒴R={(u,φ)∈𝒴:‖(u,φ)‖𝒴≤R},\mathcal{Y}_{R}=\{(u,\varphi)\in\mathcal{Y}:\|(u,\varphi)\|_{\mathcal{Y}}\leq R\},

and for any given (u,φ)∈𝒴R(u,\varphi)\in\mathcal{Y}_{R} we define a map Λ\Lambda by

where (w(u,φ),ψ(u,φ))(w^{(u,\varphi)},\psi^{(u,\varphi)}) is the solution of (6.6) with the control h(u,φ)h^{(u,\varphi)}.

Our aim is to show that for some R>0R>0, for any (u,φ)∈𝒴R(u,\varphi)\in\mathcal{Y}_{R}, Λ⁡(u,φ)∈YR\Lambda(u,\varphi)\in Y_{R} and the map Λ:𝒴R→𝒴R\Lambda:\mathcal{Y}_{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{R} is a contraction. Then the Banach fixed point theorem gives Theorem 1.4.

by choosing

(w⁡(T,⋅),ψ⁡(T,⋅))=(0,0)inL2​(0,1).\left(w(T,\cdot),\psi(T,\cdot)\right)=(0,0)\quad\mathrm{in}\quad L^{2}(0,1).

This proves the local null-controllability of the nonlinear system (1.6).

7. Further remarks and open problems

In view of our results, a few questions arise naturally and we mention them here for future investigations.

Non-constant steady state: In this article, we study the controllability of (1.2) around a certain steady state (u¯,ϕ¯)(\bar{u},\bar{\phi}), where ϕ¯\bar{\phi} is a constant and (u¯,ϕ¯)(\bar{u},\bar{\phi}) satisfies the conditions mentioned in Remark 1.1. It would be more interesting to consider the steady state satisfying (1.4) and both u¯\bar{u} and ϕ¯\bar{\phi} are non-constant functions of space variable. Then the system around (u¯,ϕ¯)(\bar{u},\bar{\phi}) is in the form:

(7.1) {wt−γ​wx​x+u¯​wx+u¯′​w=γ1​ψx+(12​ϕ¯2​ϕ¯′−ϕ¯′−ϕ¯′′)​ψ−ϕ¯′​ψx​x+N~1​(w,ψ)+χ𝒪1​h1,in ​QT,ψt+ψx​x​x​x+γ2​ψx​x+(u¯−24​ϕ¯​ϕ¯′)​ψx−(24​ϕ¯′2+2​ϕ¯​ϕ¯′′)​ψ=−ϕ′​w+N~2​(w,ψ)+χ𝒪2​h2,in ​QT,w(t,0)=0,w(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),ψx​(t,0)=0,ψx​(t,1)=0,ψx​x​x​(t,0)=0,ψx​x​x​(t,1)=0t∈(0,T),w(0,x)=w0(x),ψ(0,x)=ψ0(x),x∈(0,1),\begin{cases}w_{t}-\gamma w_{xx}+\bar{u}w_{x}+\bar{u}^{\prime}w=\gamma_{1}\psi_{x}+(12\bar{\phi}^{2}\bar{\phi}^{\prime}-\bar{\phi}^{\prime}-\bar{\phi}^{\prime\prime})\psi-\bar{\phi}^{\prime}\psi_{xx}+\widetilde{N}_{1}(w,\psi)+\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{1}}h_{1},&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ \psi_{t}+\psi_{xxxx}+\gamma_{2}\psi_{xx}+(\bar{u}-24\bar{\phi}\bar{\phi}^{\prime})\psi_{x}-(24\bar{\phi}^{\prime 2}+2\bar{\phi}\bar{\phi}^{\prime\prime})\psi=-\phi^{\prime}w+\widetilde{N}_{2}(w,\psi)+\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{2}}h_{2},&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ w(t,0)=0,\ w(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ \psi_{x}(t,0)=0,\ \psi_{x}(t,1)=0,\quad\psi_{xxx}(t,0)=0,\ \psi_{xxx}(t,1)=0&t\in(0,T),\\ w(0,x)=w_{0}(x),\,\psi(0,x)=\psi_{0}(x),&x\in(0,1),\end{cases}

where N~1\widetilde{N}_{1} and N~2\widetilde{N}_{2} are nonlinear terms. Here h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} are controls acting in any open subsets 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} of (0,1)(0,1) respectively. Comparing (1.6), it can be observed that in (7.1)1\eqref{gen non lin}_{1}, a term involving ψx​x\psi_{xx} is present whereas a term involving ww is present in (7.1)2\eqref{gen non lin}_{2}. Thus, the coupling between the equations are stronger than that of (1.6) and this makes the problem more challenging. The available Carleman inequality may not be easily adaptable to this case because of this strong coupling. Moreover, if the controllability result can be obtained, it will be interesting to investigate if the controllability can be obtained using a minimal number of controls.

It is interesting to study whether one can establish a local controllability result when the control acts in the second-order parabolic equation. It is worth mentioning that the work [5] focused on this control issue for the stabilized KS equation by controlling through the heat equation. The main ingredient of their work is to explore a new Carleman inequality associated to the KS (fourth order) equation with nonhomogeneous boundary data and source terms. The first step for this problem related to the Cahn-Hilliard-Burgers’ equation will be to investigate whether this type of Carleman inequality holds for the Cahn-Hilliard equation.

Multi-dimensional case: The immediate interest would be to study the controllability of the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes equation (1.1) in higher dimension. But it seems that a major obstacle to use our method to obtain the controllability of CHNS is the Carleman estimate for (1.1)1−(1.1)2\eqref{gen}_{1}-\eqref{gen}_{2} with the boundary conditions (1.1)6\eqref{gen}_{6}. The Carleman inequality for this case is very much related to that of the Cahn-Hilliard equation as mentioned in [19, Section 5.2]. As indicated in [19, Section 5.2], the required weight function to obtain the Carleman inequality for the Cahn-Hilliard equation with this certain boundary condition is not available and hence obtaining the inequality is still an open problem. Thus, to study the controllability of the CHNS model in higher dimension will need a different approach or an adaptation of the Carleman inequality in this set-up.

Considering different potential FF: In this article we have considered the double well potential of regular type; indeed a particular example of a regular potential given in (1.3). For diffuse interface systems modeled by these equations, a potential of singular type is more physically and thermodynamically relevant. We note that CHNS system for well-posedness as well as optimal control are well studied in the literature for the following singular potential called as logarithmic potential

(7.2) Fl​o​g​(s)=θ2​((1+s)​log⁡(1+s)+(1−s)​log⁡(1−s))+θc2​(1−s2)s∈(−1,1),0<θ<θc,\displaystyle F_{log}(s)=\frac{\theta}{2}\big((1+s)\log(1+s)+(1-s)\log(1-s)\big)+\frac{\theta_{c}}{2}(1-s^{2})\quad s\in(-1,1),\quad 0<\theta<\theta_{c},

where θ\theta and θc\theta_{c} are proportional to absolute and critical temperature, respectively. Obvious extension of the current work is to consider logarithmic potential. Note that Fl​o​gF_{log} has singularities at −1,+1-1,+1. Hence deriving corresponding linearized system similar to (7.1) system itself will be challenging. One will have to follow a general treatment for such problems via approximating the singular potential by sequence of regular potentials. However for controllability results the convergence arguments may need careful treatment.

Boundary control problems: Another interesting aspect can be addressing the boundary null controllability problem for the Cahn-Hilliard-Burgers’ equation. In [7], a local null controllability result for a system coupling KS-KdV and heat equations has been established using three boundary controls acting at the left end of the spatial domain (0,1)(0,1). This naturally raises the question of whether a similar controllability result could be achieved for the system considered in this paper. A challenging problem is whether the controllability result can be improved using less number of controls on the boundary. It is well-known that the usual Carleman estimate is not effective to explore the boundary controllability problem for coupled system with less number of control than variables as we do not have the interaction of the boundary terms for the associated adjoint system to absorb the unusual observation terms from the joint Carleman estimate. Thus, this question offers promising avenues for further research.

In this section we prove the following result:

Proposition A.1.

Let γ>0,\gamma>0, T>0T>0. Assume f∈L2​(0,T,H01​(0,1)),f\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}_{0}(0,1)), and u¯∈H2​(0,1)∩H01​(0,1).\bar{u}\in H^{2}(0,1)\cap H^{1}_{0}(0,1). Then the equation

(A.1) {zt−γ​zx​x−u¯​zx=f in ​(0,T)×(0,1),z⁡(t,0)=z⁡(t,1)=0 in ​(0,T),z⁡(0,x)=0 in ​(0,1).\begin{cases}z_{t}-\gamma z_{xx}-\bar{u}z_{x}=f&\text{ in }(0,T)\times(0,1),\\ z(t,0)=z(t,1)=0&\text{ in }(0,T),\\ z(0,x)=0&\text{ in }(0,1).\end{cases}

has a unique solution z∈L2​(0,T,H3​(0,1))z\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{3}(0,1)) and it satisfies the following estimate

Proof.

(A.3) {z~t−γ​z~x​x−u¯​z~x+λ​z~=f~ in ​(0,T)×(0,1),z~​(t,0)=z~​(t,1)=0 in ​(0,T),z~​(0,x)=0 in ​(0,1),\begin{cases}\widetilde{z}_{t}-\gamma\widetilde{z}_{xx}-\bar{u}\widetilde{z}_{x}+\lambda\widetilde{z}=\widetilde{f}&\text{ in }(0,T)\times(0,1),\\ \widetilde{z}(t,0)=\widetilde{z}(t,1)=0&\text{ in }(0,T),\\ \widetilde{z}(0,x)=0&\text{ in }(0,1),\end{cases}

where

f~​(t,x)={e−λ​t​f​(t,x)∀(t,x)∈(0,T)×(0,1)0∀(t,x)∈(T,∞)×(0,1),\widetilde{f}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}e^{-\lambda t}f(t,x)&\forall\,(t,x)\in(0,T)\times(0,1)\\ 0&\forall\,(t,x)\in(T,\infty)\times(0,1),\end{array}\right.

and ff is any given function in L2​(0,T,H01​(0,1))L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}_{0}(0,1)).

The linear operator associated to (A.3) in H01​(0,1)H^{1}_{0}(0,1) is given by

𝒟(𝒜1)={z~∈H3(0,1)∣z~(0)=0=z~(1),z~′′(0)=0=z~′′(1)},𝒜1z~=γz~′′+u¯z~′−λz~,z~∈𝒟(𝒜1).\begin{array}[]{l}\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_{1})=\{\widetilde{z}\in H^{3}(0,1)\mid\widetilde{z}(0)=0=\widetilde{z}(1),\quad\widetilde{z}^{\prime\prime}(0)=0=\widetilde{z}^{\prime\prime}(1)\},\\ \mathcal{A}_{1}\widetilde{z}=\gamma\widetilde{z}^{\prime\prime}+\bar{u}\widetilde{z}^{\prime}-\lambda\widetilde{z},\quad\widetilde{z}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_{1}).\end{array}

Now introducing z⁡(t,x)=eλ​t​z~​(t,x)z(t,x)=e^{\lambda t}\widetilde{z}(t,x), we obtain that z∈L2​(0,T,H3​(0,1))∩H1​(0,T,H01​(0,1))z\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{3}(0,1))\cap H^{1}(0,T;H^{1}_{0}(0,1)) is the unique solution of (A.1) satisfying
